content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the backdoor vulnerability of different DNN architectures including CNNs, vision transformers (ViTs), and ResMLP. By running three representative attacks BadNets, HTBA and WaNet, the authors find that ViTs are more vulnerable to backdoor attacks, especially its self-attention mechanism. A trigger localization and blocking-based defense are also presented to improve the robustness of DNNs to backdoor attacks. The findings revealed in this paper can help understand the weakness of transformers to backdoor attacks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. An early study of backdoor attack/defense on vision transformers (besides a few preprints on arXiv).
2. Thorough experiments and comparisons between different types of neural architecture.
3. Defenses have also been explored.

Weaknesses:
1. Since only three attacks are tested, the conclusions drawn from the experiments are not convincing enough. For instance, in Table, it seems that ViTs are only vulnerable to patch-based attacks like BadNets. The ASR of WaNet on CaiT is only 29.30%. The ASR on ViT-Based of HTBA is only 61.40%, 20% lower than that on CaiT. Thre are also other similar inconsistent conclusions among the attacks and architectures. More attacks need to be tested, similar to a recent defense [1] that tested 10 different attacks to draw a consistent conclusion.

2. The proposed defenses have obvious flaws, i.e., they are limited to patch-based attacks. It is also not clear why existing backdoor defenses are not evaluated with transformers, since the main purpose of this work is empirical understanding.

3. The reason why self-attention is more vulnerable to backdoor attacks is not very clear. And how can we improve backdoor robustness while still using self-attention? 

[1] Li, Yige, et al. "Anti-backdoor learning: Training clean models on poisoned data." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 14900-14912.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing of this paper can be improved. The overall presentation is quite clear, the experiments are moderately novel. Reproduccbility is good.
content.summary_of_the_review: Interesting experiments, good attempt but not very convincing due to limited attacks tested, inconsistent results, no understanding of existing defenses, and needs more understanding of the vulnerability of self-attention to different types of backdoors.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
**"Consider more attacks"**: We would like to point out that [1] experiments with only 4 backdoor attacks with a 12 label ImageNet subset. Compared to that, we use the full-ImageNet for our experiments. Hence, comparing the number of attacks considered in other papers without considering the dataset size is not fair. We believe the number of attacks considered in our experiments are enough to draw conclusions. 

[1] Li, Yige, et al. "Anti-backdoor learning: Training clean models on poisoned data." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 14900-14912.


**"Limited to patch-based attacks and existing defenses"**: In Table 5, we show results on WaNet attack which is a stealth based non-patch based attack. We would also like to emphasize that we are not claiming novelty on the defense and our novelty lies in showing that highlighting the patch based trigger is an inherent property of vision transformers, which is not present in CNNs.

We show results in supplementary for an existing defense [a]. But the paper reports results on MNIST, CIFAR10 and GTSRB and we found that the defense is not effective on ImageNet.

[a] Gao, Yansong, et al. "Strip: A defence against trojan attacks on deep neural networks." Proceedings of the 35th Annual Computer Security Applications Conference. 2019.


**"Improve backdoor robustness for self-attention"**: This needs more investigation and is beyond the scope of this paper. To improve robustness while using self attention, Table 4 shows our experiments on attention based blocking or token dropping which lead to a drop in ASR without using the defense.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper conducts a comparative study of the resistance of different DNN
architectures (i.e., ViT, VNN, ResMLP) to backdoor attacks. It demonstrates
that vision transformers are more vulnerable to backdoor attacks than CNNs. It
also observes that interpretation techniques can reveal backdoor triggers
effectively in vision transformers but not in CNNs. Based on this observation,
it designs a test-time image-blocking defense against backdoor attacks to
improve the robustness of vision transformers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The finding that vision transformers are more vulnerable to backdoor attacks than CNNs is interesting.
Its comparative study includes different model architectures (i.e., CNN, Vision transformer, ResMLP).

Experiments cannot give a conclusive claim.
Defense is not novel.
Discussion on related attacks is missing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The finding that vision transformers are more vulnerable to backdoor attacks
than CNNs is interesting. Its comparative study includes different model
architectures (i.e., CNN, Vision transformer, ResMLP).

This paper's backdoor attack setting is inconsistent with existing work and
common practice. Thus, I have doubts about the observation and experiment
results. Section 3 claims that poisoned models' attack success rate (ASR)
should be high, while this paper uses low ASR attacks (i.e., all ASRs are
lower than 70%). I suspect this is because it only uses the poisoning rate as
0.05% of the entire dataset, which leads to low ASRs. It is not a common
practice in previous works, which considers poisoning at least 0.5% of the
dataset to ensure the ASR can be over 90%. As a result, the comparative
analysis of different models' vulnerabilities of backdoor attacks is based on
an unsuccessful or weak attack setting. In this setting, the poor attack
performance in CNNs can give rise to low poison rates and unsuccessful
backdoor injections. I think the argument that vision transformers are more
vulnerable to backdoor attacks is not convincing. 

The defense method of this paper only considers a specific type of patch
trigger, which different types of trigger patterns can easily bypass. Section
4 shows that interpretation techniques like Grad-Cam can localize the backdoor
of patch triggers in vision transformers. The success of this defense depends
on this locality characteristic. But existing works like the Blended attack
[3], Filter attacks [4], and other feature space attacks consider backdoor
attacks with pervasive trigger patterns. For these attacks, the ground truth
triggers do not even have a locality. Existing work suggests that these
triggers can not be localized in interpretation maps since they are global in
the whole image, bypassing this type of defense. 

Besides, this defense requires the backdoor features to be visible in the
pixel space. However, works using human-invisible patterns as backdoor
triggers, like [5, 6]. These backdoor attacks can also bypass its defense
mechanism since their triggers are less-likely to expose features in the
interpretation maps. The design and evaluation do not consider the backdoor
mentioned above attacks. We cannot evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed
defense under more advanced and adaptive attacks.

[1] Gu et al. "BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain" IEEE Access 2019
[2] Liu et al. "Trojaning Attack on Neural Networks" NDSS 2018
[3] Chen et al. "Targeted Backdoor Attacks on Deep Learning Systems Using Data Poisoning." arXiv 2017
[4] Liu et al. "Abs: Scanning neural networks for backdoors by artificial brain stimulation" CCS 2019
[5] Li et al. "Invisible Backdoor Attack with Sample-Specific Triggers" ICCV 2021
[6] Zhang et al. "Poison Ink: Robust and Invisible Backdoor Attack" TIP 2022
content.summary_of_the_review:
​The backdoor attack setting in this paper is weak and inconsistent with
existing work. Many existing works can potentially bypass its defense method.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
**"Poisoning rate is inconsistent with previous work"**: We would like to emphasize that increasing the poison rate from 0.05\% to 0.5\% implies that the number of poisons increases from 600 to 6000 images. Each category in ImageNet has ~1300 images, so adding 6000 poison is not practical. To the best of our knowledge, 0.5\% poisoning rate is not a standard choice in backdoor attack literature. Our observations and results are not necessarily dependent on the poisoning rate.

**"Effectiveness of defense against non-local attacks"**: In table 5, we show results on WaNet attack which is not patch based and is a non-local attack.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors investigated the effectiveness of backdoor attacks in transformer architectures and compare the result with traditional CNNs. They explored the attention mechanism of the transformer architecture against the backdoor attack in the hope to encourage the community to develop more robust models. The authors conducted experiments with three different backdoor attacks, BadNet, HTBA, and WaNet to examine the attention mechanism of the transformer architecture against the backdoor attacks. Results show that the vision transformer architecture (ViT) is weakest against backdoor attacks, whereas ResMLP which has the Feed Forward Networks (FNN) is strongest. This paper claimed that the attention of mechanism has a huge impact on against the backdoor attacks and Vision Transformers are not robust. They also found that the interpretation map for transformers is more effective than the one for CNNs, this intrigues the author to develop a blocking mechanism to improve the robustness of the model.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper empirically studies the vulnerability of ViTs and CNNs against backdoor attacks. The paper observes that ViTs are less robust than CNNs and for patch-based triggers, ViTs attend closer to the trigger on the image when making predictions. Based on this observation, the paper proposes a trigger-blocking technique for the salient parts of the images. The paper shows that this technique works well for the patch-based trigger (Badnets) and Wanet on Imagenet dataset.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is well-written and the motivation is well-described. The proposed defense is effective in lowering ASR. The experiment in Imagenet is different than some relevant works. However, I think there are some major weaknesses:

- The novelty is limited compared to the existing/related works. For example, Doan et al. 2022 have already demonstrated the backdoor risks in several datasets, including the related Tiny Imagenet. The blocking defense also resembles a technique used in Doan et al. 2022, although blocking in the paper is done on the salient part. 
- I think that the paper should experiments with all datasets that are used in backdoor studies (e.g., GTSRB, MNIST), not just Imagenet to demonstrate the generalization of this method. This is to improve the novelty and contribution of the paper.
- Some experiments are not clearly motivated. For example, why freezing the final layer of the pre-trained models in fine-tuning? Most other works do not do this to gain good performance on the target tasks.
- The statement in 3.1 is strong (ViT is less robust compared to CNNs) given the current experiment. To the best of my knowledge, if it's 1-1 source target backdoor (images from one source class with trigger will be classified as one target class), the ASR is always less than the accuracy of the model on clean data. Thus, ViTs' clean-data accuracies in this experiment are much better than those of ResMLP and other CNNs, it's natural that their ASRs are also higher. I'm confident that if the paper includes the bigger CNNs such as Big Transfer (BiT), their ASRs will also be  higher and comparable to those of ViTs. In summary, the existing experimental design in this section is flawed.
- Some other places, like in "self attention vs MLP", the paper replaces the Attention block in ViT with an MLP block, and concludes that "MLP provides a major boost in terms of robustness" is very questionable and not concise. The attention block is a well-designed architecture and has been validated to work well in several domains; replacing it with MLP may mess with other parts of the model, thus resulting in a decrease in both clean-data accuracy and ASRs... Therefore, the conclusion is not well supported by the evidence in these experiments.
- Several other experimental choices are not well-designed. For example, WaNet attack is known to cause local artifacts that act like a patch-based trigger. The paper should also study other types of attacks that act on the entire image (for example, ReFool, SIG...). Also calling WaNet "non-trigger" is not correct. In fact, all backdoor attacks have "triggers", it's just that WaNet has triggers that are blended well into the images.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written; however, the novelty of the paper is limited. The paper seems to include enough details to reproduce the work.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper studies an interesting direction. However, the novelty is limited because of the not-so-well experimental designs and several non-precise and not well supported claims.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the feedback, please find our response below:


**"Limited novelty compared to Doan et al. 2022"**: We want to emphasize that our novelty is presenting the differences between CNNs and Transformers, and how architectural building blocks such as self-attention affect the robustness of the model. We believe that ours is the first work that conducts such a comprehensive set of experiments across larger set of architectures and a complex setting such as ImageNet. Doan et al. is an unpublished arxiv work which has slight similarity in terms of defense but we are not claiming novelty on that. Our contribution is showing self attention in Vision Transformers can lead to interpretation maps that easily highlight the trigger, which is not seen in CNNs.



**"Adding experiments with GTSRB and MNIST"**: We believe it is best to study backdoor attacks on large and complex datasets, e.g. ImageNet. The insights gained from experiments on ImageNet models might have more practical applicability than the ones from MNIST and GTSRB. 


**"Freezing the backbone"**: We are considering a backdoor threat model where the victim downloads poisoned data from the internet when finetuning a pre-trained model for their custom task. We believe this threat model to be realistic and fair given that most practitioners simply adapt existing pretrained models. Hidden Trigger Backdoor Attack (HTBA) is shown to be effective in transfer learning scenarios where the backbone remains frozen. To be consistent, we use the same setting for all attacks to provide a fair comparison.  


**"Correlation of ASR and clean accuracy"**: We strongly disagree with the reviewer that our experiments are flawed and do not believe such a correlation exists between ASR and the clean accuracy of the model. We would also like to emphasize that other architectures such as PatchConv have higher clean accuracy, but it does not mean the ASR is also higher. To the best of our knowledge, we are not aware of such a study or reference and will be glad to discuss it if references are provided. 


**"Replacing self attention with MLP"**: We conduct this controlled study where self-attention is replaced with MLP to understand the robustness of various architectural blocks. The statement "mess with other parts of the model" seems vague since ResMLP and other well cited works on FFN perform such comparisons as well. We agree with the reviewer that attention block is a well designed architecture and is validated to work well in several domains, but its effects on backdoor robustness has not been studied before.


**"WaNet attack creates local artifacts and is patch-based"**: We strongly believe the objective of WaNet attack is to not create "local artifacts". As demonstrated in the WaNet original paper, the residual added to create the attack is spread all over the image and is not localized, hence it is a different attack compared to a patch-based trigger. In fact, in section 4.5 of the paper, they demonstrate that a GradCAM visualization for poisoned images does not differ from clean images, showing that the effect of the trigger is not localized to a small region. Although there exists many backdoor attacks in literature with distinct threat models, it is impossible for us to consider all of them. We believe that the 3 backdoor attacks considered, BadNets (dirty label patch attack), HTBA (clean label patch attack) and WaNet (dirty label stealth or human invisible attack) broadly encapsulates the family of attacks. We will change the writing to show that WaNet is also a trigger based attack.
